newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Attack on Iranian centre in Pakistan kills seven.
newsitem.headline: Attack on Iranian centre in Pakistan kills seven.

text.p: Gunmen attacked Iran's cultural centre in the central Pakistani city of Multan on Thursday, killing seven people, including its director, and wounding at least one, officials said.
They said several men armed with assault rifles had forced their way into the cultural centre at around 1 p.m. (0800 GMT) and started shooting indiscriminately.
They said the gunmen had shot dead seven people in the centre, including its Iranian director, Muhammad Ali Rahimi.

Last month a crowd of Sunni Moslem militants ransacked and burned the Iranian cultural centre in Lahore, capital of Punjab province, after a bomb explosion in the city killed Zia-ur-Rahman Faruqi, leader of the Sipah-i-Sahaba Pakistan (SSP) faction.
SSP followers blamed Shi'ite Moslem militants for the Lahore bombing, which killed 26 people and wounded about 90. Shi'ite groups denied they were involved.
Allama Sajid Naqvi, the Islamabad-based leader of the Shi'ite Tehrik-i-Jafria Pakistan (TJP) group, said SSP activists had carried out Thursday's attack on the Iranian cultural centre.
There was no immediate comment from the SSP.

Violence between militant groups among Pakistan's majority Sunnis and minority Shi'ites cost at least 170 lives last year. Shi'ites form about 15 percent of Pakistan's population of over 130 million, but are the majority in neighbouring Iran.
Local officials said several men posing as Shi'ites had visited Rahimi on Wednesday and asked permission to hold a Moslem celebration in the cultural centre.

The same men arrived there on Thursday in two cars and on two motorcycles, threw hot chili powder into the eyes of seven or eight policemen guarding the building, snatched their weapons, swept inside and started shooting.
Before escaping, the assailants chanted anti-Shi'ite slogans, police and officials said.
Iranian Foreign Minister Ali Akbar Velayati is expected to visit Pakistan next week to deliver invitations for an Islamic summit conference to be held in Tehran in December.

Velayati, who would be the first foreign minister of an Islamic country to visit Pakistan since Nawaz Sharif was elected prime minister this month, was also expected to discuss regional issues, including Afghanistan and the Kashmir dispute.
Iran has in the past urged the Pakistani government to protect Shi'ites from attack by what it calls terrorists.
